name: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
title: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
answer: Federated sharing of sensitive data covers arrangements where separate organizations or repositories keep data in place and exchange only models, statistics, or encrypted intermediate results. It applies to health records, genomic data, financial records, and other personal or confidential datasets that cannot be pooled into one central store. The aim is to support research and analysis across institutions without moving raw records. In research data and repositories, this touches data access committees, metadata standards, and reproducibility.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Federated sharing of sensitive data covers arrangements where separate organizations or repositories keep data in place and exchange only models, statistics, or encrypted intermediate results. It applies to health records, genomic data, financial records, and other personal or confidential datasets that cannot be pooled into one central store. The aim is to support research and analysis across institutions without moving raw records. In research data and repositories, this touches data access committees, metadata standards, and reproducibility.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The infrastructure usually includes a coordinating server or peer-to-peer network, local compute nodes inside each data holder, and secure communication channels. Common building blocks are containerized analysis environments, federated learning frameworks, secure multi-party computation libraries, and hardware-backed trusted execution environments. Repositories may provide persistent identifiers, metadata catalogues, and audit logs rather than central data storage. Network bandwidth, identity federation, and key management are practical constraints.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical project defines a common schema or model, distributes code to each site, and runs local training or queries. Sites return only agreed outputs, such as model updates, aggregate statistics, or encrypted shares. Secure aggregation, differential privacy, and output checking reduce what can be inferred from those returns. Results are then combined by a coordinator or through a protocol, and the process is documented for review.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Each data holder retains control and must have a lawful basis, consent, or ethics approval for the specific use. Data sharing agreements, access committees, and privacy impact assessments set the rules, while provenance records track which datasets and code versions contributed. Risks include re-identification, inference attacks, model inversion, and unintended leakage through repeated queries. Repositories and researchers need clear audit trails, retention rules, and procedures for withdrawal or correction.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward standardized federated protocols, reusable privacy budgets, and better tooling for non-specialists. Regulators and funders increasingly expect documented privacy safeguards alongside scientific results. More repositories may offer federated analysis as a service, with metadata and provenance built in. The open questions are how to compare privacy guarantees across sites and how to make cross-border collaboration practical.
